title: Product/Market Fit: what it feels like and the numbers that define it
summary: Jason Cohen defines PMF as a felt shift from push to pull, backed by three tests: sudden sustained growth, low churn, and critical mass. He shows the same linear-then-steeper-linear curve across bootstrapped, VC-funded, viral and media businesses, and argues high churn means no fit.

principles.text: PMF is unmistakable: it's a shift from pushing for each customer to being pulled by demand. If you're unsure, you don't have it.
principles.quote: there is no doubt when you have it**. (If you're not sure whether you have Product/Market Fit, you don't.)

principles.text: Define PMF as three things together: easy growth, high retention, and critical mass.
principles.quote: **I define Product/Market Fit as _all_ of the following:**

principles.text: Churn must be under 3%/mo for B2B or 5%/mo for B2C. Customers leaving in droves means no fit, however fast you grow.
principles.quote: cancellation higher than 3% for B2B or 5% for B2C indicates a lack of Product/Market Fit

principles.text: PMF growth is linear, then a sudden bend to a steeper linear slope, not exponential. This holds for bootstrapped, VC-funded, viral and media businesses.
principles.quote: Revenue growing linearly, slowly, often for about two years, then in a moment--Product/Market Fit--when it suddenly turns upward, and continues growing at that new trajectory.

principles.text: High churn caps growth: churn scales with your base while acquisition doesn't, so cancellations eventually win the race.
principles.quote: 5%/mo" definitionally grows in lock-step with your total size, but marketing and sales does not continue to automatically grow just because your company is bigger.

principles.text: Judge fit by customer behavior, not dollars. PMF also brings a crushing workload, so hire ahead of need.
principles.quote: Don't get distracted by dollars. Pay attention to customer behavior.
